summary: Sirach 14 begins with blessings on a person whose speech and conscience do not leave him in despair. It then warns against the miser who gathers wealth but cannot enjoy or share it, urges generous enjoyment before death, and closes by picturing wisdom as someone to seek, watch, lodge near, and shelter under.
whyItMatters: The chapter joins two major concerns of Sirach: disciplined conduct with money and disciplined pursuit of wisdom. It treats mortality as a reason for generosity and wise attention, not for hoarding.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made later by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson's translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180-175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal study, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact poetic sayings and direct teaching.

outline.heading: Blessed speech and hope
outline.note: The chapter opens by blessing the person who has not slipped with the mouth, whose soul does not condemn him, and who has not given up hope.

outline.heading: The misery of miserliness
outline.note: Riches are shown as useless for a stingy or covetous person who gathers for others, withholds from himself, and lacks even bread at his table.

outline.heading: Use and give before death
outline.note: The teacher tells his son to treat himself well, bring offerings, help friends, and not let a good share pass by, because death and Hades limit future enjoyment.

outline.heading: The common fate of flesh
outline.note: Human life is compared to a garment that grows old and leaves on a tree that fall and grow, while every work and its builder pass away.

outline.heading: Seeking wisdom closely
outline.note: The chapter ends by blessing the person who meditates on wisdom and stays near her house, shelter, branches, and glory.

keyVerses.text: Blessed is he whose soul does not condemn him, and who has not given up hope.
keyVerses.why: This verse frames the opening concern with inner judgment and hope, not only outward behavior.

keyVerses.text: A miser begrudges bread, and it is lacking at his table.
keyVerses.why: It compresses the warning about miserliness into an image of wealth that still fails to nourish ordinary life.

keyVerses.text: Do good to your friends before you die. According to your ability, reach out and give to them.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the chapter's positive alternative to hoarding: timely generosity within one's means.

keyVerses.text: Blessed is the man who meditates on wisdom, and who reasons by his understanding.
keyVerses.why: It begins the final movement from wealth and mortality to the active pursuit of wisdom.

themes: the passing of flesh and work

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with the mouth?
questions.answer: Verse 1 blesses the person who has not slipped with his mouth, and verse 2 links this to a soul that does not condemn him and has not given up hope. The chapter does not explain a specific incident; it starts with speech as one place where wisdom or failure becomes visible.

questions.question: What is a miser in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter portrays a miser as someone whose relationship to goods is distorted. He gathers by denying himself, does not enjoy his possessions, turns away from souls, is not satisfied with his portion, and even begrudges bread at his table.

questions.question: Is the chapter telling people simply to spend money on themselves?
questions.answer: No. The counsel includes treating yourself well, bringing worthy offerings to the Lord, doing good to friends, and giving according to your ability. The target is not restraint as such, but a hoarding or grudging life that neither enjoys goods nor shares them.

questions.question: Why does death become part of money advice?
questions.answer: Verses 12-16 argue that death will not wait and that labor and goods may be left to another. The point inside this chapter is practical and sobering: mortality makes hoarding look foolish and makes present generosity urgent.

questions.question: What does Hades mean here?
questions.answer: The chapter mentions Hades twice, first with the statement that its covenant has not been shown to the reader, and then by saying there is no seeking of luxury in Hades. Within this chapter, Hades is connected with death and with the end of ordinary earthly enjoyment; the text does not pause to give a full map of the afterlife.

questions.question: Is verse 16 a hard verse because it sounds like luxury is being approved?
questions.answer: It can be hard because the sentence says, "Give, take, and treat yourself well," and explains this by the absence of luxury in Hades. Readers differ over how broadly to take this counsel: some stress sober enjoyment of one's share, while others stress the surrounding commands to give and do good. The chapter itself keeps enjoyment and generosity together.

questions.question: What is the image of leaves on a tree doing?
questions.answer: Verse 18 compares generations of flesh and blood to leaves on a thick tree: some are shed and some grow. It makes the mortality of verse 17 concrete by placing each life within a larger pattern of coming and going.

questions.question: Why is wisdom described like a woman with a house, windows, doors, shelter, and branches?
questions.answer: Verses 20-27 personify wisdom as someone whose ways can be considered, whose paths can be watched, and whose shelter can protect. The chapter uses this imagery to describe persistent nearness to wisdom, not a casual interest in wise sayings.

questions.question: How do the two halves of the chapter fit together?
questions.answer: The first major section warns against wealth that cannot be enjoyed or shared, especially in light of death. The final section redirects desire toward wisdom, pictured as a sheltering presence. Together they contrast a closed, grudging life with a life that gives, receives, and seeks wisdom closely.

glossary.def: In this chapter, a person who clings to goods in a way that harms both himself and others; he begrudges even bread at his table.
The place or state associated here with death, where the chapter says there is no seeking of luxury.
A phrase used for human generations that come to an end and are followed by others.
The desired guide in the final section, pictured as someone whose ways, paths, house, shelter, branches, and glory can be sought.
